title: Breakfast at the cafeteria
goal: Say you haven't had breakfast and thank Sēf when he offers to pay
tip: Past recap: trayyagt? 'have you had breakfast?' and trayyagt 'I've had breakfast' sound the same, like shirabt; ma trayyagt = I haven't. Endings recap: ḥsāb + -i gives ʿala ḥsābi, 'on my account', so 'it's on me'.
dialogue: Morning, man. Have you had breakfast?
صباح النور. لا، ما تريقت. أنا يوعان
ṣabāḥ in-nūr. la, ma trayyagt. ana yōʿān
Morning. No, I haven't. I'm hungry.
يلا، الريوق على حسابي. كرك وخبز وبيض؟
yalla, ir-riyūg ʿala ḥsābi. karak w khubz w bēẓ?
Come on, breakfast's on me. Karak, bread and eggs?
Thanks! The karak here is good, isn't it?
items: I've had breakfast / have you had breakfast? (to a man)
to a woman: trayyagti?; I haven't: ma trayyagt
a woman: yōʿāna (يوعانة); you'll see written جوعان
karak (strong tea boiled with milk and spices)
reply: allāh yʿāfīk; to a woman: allāh yʿāfīch
culture: Karak is strong black tea boiled with milk, sugar and cardamom. Small cafeterias all over Dubai sell it all day, and many people order it without getting out of the car. Among friends, offering to pay (ʿala ḥsābi) is normal; the other person often protests, or thanks them and pays next time.

title: At the supermarket
goal: Shop with Maryam for the office breakfast: say what you need and ask a woman what she wants
tip: Endings recap: nāgiṣ 'missing' + -na gives shu nāgiṣna? 'what do we need?'. To a woman the verb ends in -īn: inti shu tabīn? (to a man: shu tabi?). inzēn means 'OK, will do', or 'OK?' tagged on the end of a request.
dialogue: باكر الريوق علينا. شو نشتري من السوبرماركت؟
bāchir ir-riyūg ʿalēna. shu nishtiri min is-sūbarmārkit?
Tomorrow breakfast is on us. What shall we buy at the supermarket?
ناقصنا حليب وخبز. وانتي شو تبين؟
nāgiṣna ḥalīb w khubz. w inti shu tabīn?
We need milk and bread. And what do you want?
abi fawākih. w khudh kīs, inzēn?
I want fruit. And take a bag, OK?
items: shu nāgiṣna? = what do we need?
OK, will do; OK? (after a request)
said when you agree to do something
from English; normal among young people

title: Ordering dinner in
goal: Greet Sēf after his shower, agree on dinner, order from a restaurant and insist on paying
tip: After a shower or a haircut say naʿīman; the reply is allāh yinʿim ʿalēk. Endings recap: ʿala ḥsābi 'on me'. Insist with la wallāh: la wallāh, hal-marra ʿalay 'no way, this time it's on me'.
dialogue: Thanks (God bless you). What shall we have for dinner?
أنا يوعان. نطلب أكل من مطعم؟
ana yōʿān. niṭlub akil min maṭʿam?
I'm hungry. Shall we order food from a restaurant?
هيه، عيش ودياي. والعشا على حسابي
hē, ʿēsh w diyāy. w il-ʿasha ʿala ḥsābi
Yes, rice and chicken. And dinner's on me.
No way, this time it's on me!
items: said to someone fresh from a shower or a haircut
to a woman: allāh yinʿim ʿalēch
we have dinner / shall we have dinner?
you'll see written دجاج too; one chicken: diyāya
no way, no really (refusing or insisting)
used when you insist, e.g. on paying

title: Lunch at Sēf's house
goal: Answer Umm Sēf's welcome, praise her cooking and say you're full
tip: To a woman, use -ich: allāh yḥayyīch, allāh yʿāfīch. tislam īdich 'bless your hand' thanks the cook; the hand is the subject, so tislam doesn't change. Past recap: shbaʿt 'I'm full'. Endings: ṣaḥnak 'your plate'.
dialogue: Welcome. Please, come and have lunch.
الله يحييج. ما شاء الله، سمك ولحم!
allāh yḥayyīch. mā shāʼ allāh, simach w laḥam!
Thank you. Wow, fish and meat!
والله شبعت. تسلم إيدج، وايد لذيذ
wallāh shbaʿt. tislam īdich, wāyid ladhīdh
Honestly, I'm full. Bless your hands, it's delicious.
items: a woman, or a feminine thing: fāẓya
thank you (to a man; lit. may you be safe)
to a woman: tislamīn (تسلمين); reply: allāh ysallmak
bless your hands (to a man who cooked or made something)
to a woman: tislam īdich (تسلم إيدج); reply: allāh ysallmak
culture: Eat, pass dishes and take your coffee cup with the right hand. A host keeps offering more even after you say you're full; saying wallāh shbaʿt, il-ḥamdu lillāh once or twice is the polite way to stop. Praise the food and thank the cook with tislam īdich.

title: Finding the metro station
goal: Ask a passer-by the way to the metro and follow directions with 'in front of' and 'behind'
tip: Place words go straight before the noun: jiddām il-mōl 'in front of the mall', wara l-maḥaṭṭa 'behind the station'. They take the same endings as nouns: jiddāmak 'in front of you', warāh 'behind it'.
grammar: prepositions of place: jiddām, wara, fōg, taḥt, yamm, barra, ṣōb + noun or ending
dialogue: Excuse me, where's the metro station?
مب بعيد. روح سيدا صوب الإشارة
mub baʿīd. rūḥ sīda ṣōb il-ishāra
It's not far. Go straight on towards the traffic lights.
At the lights, do I go right?
No, left. You'll see the mall in front of you.
And the station's behind the mall?
Yes, behind it. Just five minutes.
items: the same word as in ʿindi 'I have'
jiddāmak = in front of you; you'll see written جدام

title: Up or down? On the metro
goal: Find the platform and the tickets with Sēf, ask where to get off and sit next to him
tip: fōg 'up, above' and taḥt 'down, below' stand alone or go before a noun: il-mitro fōg 'the metro's upstairs', taḥt il-mōl 'under the mall'. yamm 'next to' takes endings too: yamm il-bāb 'by the door', yammi 'next to me'.
grammar: prepositions of place: jiddām, wara, fōg, taḥt, yamm, barra, ṣōb + noun or ending
dialogue: Come on, let's take the metro.
OK. Is the metro upstairs or downstairs?
فوق. بس التذكرة تحت، يم الباب
fōg. bas it-tadhkara taḥt, yamm il-bāb
Upstairs. But you get the ticket downstairs, by the door.
المترو مب زحمة اليوم. وين ننزل؟
il-mitro mub zaḥma l-yōm. wēn ninzil?
The metro isn't crowded today. Where do we get off?
في محطة المول. تعال، اقعد يمي
fi maḥaṭṭat il-mōl. taʿāl, igʿid yammi
At the mall station. Come, sit next to me.
items: we get on / let's take (the bus, the metro)
we get off / let's get off
to a woman: igʿidi; UAE also uses yalas (يلس) 'sat' for this verb
yammi = next to me; yammak = next to you; you'll also hear jamb (جنب)

title: Where are you? On the phone
goal: Find Maryam outside the mall by phone: say where you are, outside or inside, and that you're coming
tip: barra 'outside' and dākhil 'inside' also go before a noun: barra l-mōl, dākhil il-mōl. yāy 'coming' works like rāyiḥ: a man says yāy, a woman yāya. To a woman the endings take -ich: minnich 'from you', asmaʿich 'I hear you'.
grammar: prepositions of place: jiddām, wara, fōg, taḥt, yamm, barra, ṣōb + noun or ending
dialogue: I'm on the way. I'm coming now.
زين. أنا برا المول، عند الباب
zēn. ana barra l-mōl, ʿind il-bāb
OK. I'm outside the mall, by the door.
ما أسمعج عدل. انتي داخل المول؟
ma asmaʿich ʿidil. inti dākhil il-mōl?
I can't hear you properly. Are you inside the mall?
No, outside! In front of the door.
انزين، أنا قريب منج. خمس دقايق
inzēn, ana garīb minnich. khams dagāyig
OK, I'm close to you. Five minutes.
items: a woman: yāya (ياية); you'll see written جاي
I can't hear you (to a man)
to a woman: ma asmaʿich (ما أسمعج)
ma asmaʿak ʿidil = I can't hear you properly

title: Bus or metro? Getting to the airport
goal: Ask Sēf how to get to the airport and compare the bus, the metro and walking
tip: chēf? 'how?' asks the same as shlōn? from u15; both are fine: chēf arūḥ il-maṭār? 'how do I get to the airport?'. Place words keep working: il-mōgif jiddām il-bēt 'the stop's in front of the house'.
grammar: prepositions of place: jiddām, wara, fōg, taḥt, yamm, barra, ṣōb + noun or ending
dialogue: Tomorrow I'm going to the airport. How do I get there?
And the bus? The stop's in front of the house.
The bus gets there, but it isn't fast.
OK, the metro. Is the station far?
لا، يم المول. خمس دقايق على ريولك
la, yamm il-mōl. khams dagāyig ʿala ryūlak
No, it's by the mall. Five minutes on foot.
items: the same as shlōn (u15); some say kēf
in a question you'll also hear walla
to a man: ʿala ryūlak; to a woman: ʿala ryūlich (على ريولج); you'll see written رجولي

title: Checkpoint 1.4: a day out with Sēf
goal: Meet Sēf and his friends: find them, suggest lunch and argue over the bill, speaking to a group
tip: Talking to a group, use intu and plural endings. Adjectives take -īn: yōʿānīn 'hungry', garībīn 'close'; yāy becomes yāyīn 'coming', and verbs take -ūn: tabūn? 'do you want?'. ḥsāb takes -na for 'us': ʿala ḥsābna 'it's on us'.
dialogue: Hi Sēf, where are you guys?
هلا فيك! ياين، نحن في المترو، قريبين
hala fīk! yāyīn, niḥin fi l-mitro, garībīn
Hi! Coming, we're on the metro, close by.
زين. انتو يوعانين؟ تبون نتغدى في المول؟
zēn. intu yōʿānīn? tabūn nitghadda fi l-mōl?
Great. Are you hungry? Do you want to have lunch at the mall?
فوق، يم السينما. والغدا على حسابي
fōg, yamm is-sīnama. w il-ghada ʿala ḥsābi
Upstairs, next to the cinema. And lunch is on me.
No way, lunch is on us!
items: to one man: inta wēn?; to one woman: inti wēn?
one man: yāy; one woman: yāya
one man: garīb; one woman: garība
one man: yōʿān; one woman: yōʿāna
to one man: tabi?; to one woman: tabīn?

title: A1 exit: where I live and who I know
goal: Tell Umm Sēf where you live, who you live with and what the area is like
tip: sākin 'living' works like rāyiḥ: a man says sākin, a woman sākna. Adjectives agree too: il-manṭiga hādya 'the area's quiet', il-jīrān ṭayybīn 'the neighbours are nice'. Endings: b-rōḥak 'on your own', aʿarfah 'I know him', aʿarfhum 'I know them'.
grammar: A1 exit: describe where I live and people I know
dialogue: In Deira, in a small flat.
Do you live on your own?
لا، ويا ربيعي. أعرفه من الجامعة
la, wiyya rbīʿi. aʿarfah min il-jāmʿa
No, with my friend. I know him from university.
mā shāʼ allāh. w il-manṭiga ḥilwa?
How lovely. And is the area nice?
هيه، هادية. والجيران طيبين، أعرفهم كلهم
hē, hādya. w il-jīrān ṭayybīn, aʿarfhum killhum
Yes, it's quiet. And the neighbours are nice, I know them all.
items: a woman: sākna (ساكنة); wēn sākin? = where do you live?
quiet, calm (with a feminine noun: area, flat)
culture: Most people living in Dubai aren't Emirati, so English is often the working language in shops and offices. Start in Arabic anyway: a few Gulf words usually change the tone of the whole conversation.
